# Tab 1

# **MAIN BARRIERS MEXICAN & CENTRAL AMERICAN IMMIGRANTS FACE WHEN STARTING BUSINESSES**

**1\. LEGAL STATUS / IMMIGRATION POLICY BARRIERS**

**Undocumented status limits access to formal employment, credit, contracts, and business licenses.**

* Roberto Gonzales explains how undocumented individuals live in a state of “legal liminality,” meaning they can work but cannot fully integrate or access systems that require legal status — including business formation, bank loans, and professional licensing (Gonzales 2011, p. 608).  
   🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/41236156](https://www.jstor.org/stable/41236156) 

**Immigration status reduces incomes and business ownership outcomes.**

* Undocumented Mexican immigrants face lower returns to education and lower wage growth, making it harder to save startup capital (Hall, Greenman, and Farkas 2010).  
   🔗 [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4235135/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4235135/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Legal status creates fear of interacting with institutions that support entrepreneurship.**

* Cecilia Menjívar describes how “legal violence” creates fear that prevents immigrants from accessing economic opportunities and formal institutions (Menjívar 2006, p. 1000).  
   🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4149494](https://www.jstor.org/stable/4149494)

**Many business support systems require SSNs, tax IDs, or legal residency.**

* The Migration Policy Institute states that lack of legal status directly restricts access to loans, banking, and government business programs.  
   🔗 [https://www.migrationpolicy.org/research/policies-support-immigrant-entrepreneurship](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/research/policies-support-immigrant-entrepreneurship?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**2\. LIMITED ACCESS TO FINANCIAL CAPITAL**

**Immigrants rely on personal savings instead of banks.**

* SBA research shows immigrant entrepreneurs are significantly less likely to receive loans from U.S. banks compared to native-born owners (Fairlie, 2012).  
   🔗 [https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/Immigrant-Entrepreneurs-Financial-Capital-Full-Report.pdf](https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/Immigrant-Entrepreneurs-Financial-Capital-Full-Report.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Latino and Mexican entrepreneurs face discrimination in lending.**

* A detailed MBDA study documents systemic lending discrimination against Latino business owners, noting large gaps in approval rates and loan amounts (Fairlie & Robb, 2008).  
   🔗 [https://www.mbda.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/files-attachments/DisparitiesinCapitalAccessReport.pdf](https://www.mbda.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/files-attachments/DisparitiesinCapitalAccessReport.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**49% of Mexican immigrants have no credit history upon arrival.**

* Migration Policy Institute reports that lack of credit limits access to capital, even for documented immigrants.  
   🔗 [https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/mexican-immigrants-united-states](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/mexican-immigrants-united-states)

**3\. LANGUAGE & CULTURAL BARRIERS**

**Language limits ability to apply for grants, loans, licenses, and permits.**

* The American Immigration Council found most disaster/relief business programs during COVID were inaccessible to immigrants due to English-only documentation (2020).  
   🔗 [https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/report/covid19-immigrant-entrepreneurs-languages](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/report/covid19-immigrant-entrepreneurs-languages?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Most U.S. business training programs do not offer Spanish-language instruction.**

* Immigrants Rising reports that first-generation Latino entrepreneurs often lack access to culturally aligned business education.  
   🔗 [https://immigrantsrising.org/wp-content/uploads/Immigrants-Rising\_Navigating-Entrepreneurship-Research-Report\_2025.pdf](https://immigrantsrising.org/wp-content/uploads/Immigrants-Rising_Navigating-Entrepreneurship-Research-Report_2025.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**4\. SOCIAL & RACIAL DISCRIMINATION**

**Mexican and Central American immigrants face racialization as “illegal,” which follows them into economic spaces.**

* Nicholas De Genova explains how Mexican and Central American immigrants become racially categorized as “illegal,” shaping their access to economic opportunity (De Genova 2004, p. 161).  
   🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3185238](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3185238)

**Latino-owned businesses receive fewer loans and smaller loan amounts than white-owned businesses.**

* SBA data confirms a wide “capital gap” for Latino entrepreneurs (SBA, 2024).  
   🔗 https://advocacy.sba.gov/2024/01/03/hispanic-business-owners-facts/

**Discrimination affects customer trust, landlord negotiations, and supplier relationships.**

* A Rutgers review found that Latino immigrant businesses face community-level discrimination that prevents expansion.  
   🔗 [https://smlr.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/Documents/Centers/WJL/MN\_SBChallenges.pdf](https://smlr.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/Documents/Centers/WJL/MN_SBChallenges.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

# Tab 4

# **MAIN BARRIERS MEXICAN AND CENTRAL AMERICAN IMMIGRANTS FACE WHEN STARTING BUSINESSES**

Everything here is from publicly accessible sources, and all quotes include links.

---

## **1\. LEGAL STATUS AND IMMIGRATION POLICY BARRIERS**

### **A. Legal status blocks full economic participation**

**Quote:**  
 “Undocumented young adults must negotiate a system that recognizes their labor but denies them full participation.”  
 (Gonzales 2011, p. 608\)  
 🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/41236156](https://www.jstor.org/stable/41236156)

**Analysis:**  
 Gonzales shows that immigrants can work, but their legal status prevents them from accessing business licenses, loans, government programs, and professional certifications. This barrier stops many Mexican and Central American immigrants from starting formal businesses and forces them to work informally.

---

### **B. Undocumented status lowers incomes and business outcomes**

**Quote:**  
 “Undocumented immigrants have significantly lower wages and lower returns to education than documented immigrants.”  
 (Hall, Greenman and Farkas 2010\)  
 🔗 [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4235135/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4235135/)

**Analysis:**  
 Because undocumented immigrants earn less, it is harder to save enough money to start a business. Even when they have education or skills, their earnings do not increase at the same rate as documented workers, creating long-term economic disadvantages.

---

### **C. Immigration law creates fear and prevents interaction with institutions**

**Quote:**  
 “Legal structures and their implementation generate vulnerability and punitive consequences for immigrants.”  
 (Menjívar 2006, p. 1000\)  
 🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4149494](https://www.jstor.org/stable/4149494)

**Analysis:**  
 Menjívar shows that fear of detention, deportation, or discrimination keeps immigrants away from banks, loan programs, government offices, and financial institutions. This fear blocks immigrant entrepreneurs from the resources needed to start and grow their businesses.

---

### **D. Legal status limits access to banks, loans, and government programs**

**Quote:**  
 “Legal status limitations restrict immigrant entrepreneurs’ access to loans, banking services, and government business programs.”  
 (Migration Policy Institute)  
 🔗 [https://www.migrationpolicy.org/research/policies-support-immigrant-entrepreneurship](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/research/policies-support-immigrant-entrepreneurship)

**Analysis:**  
 The Migration Policy Institute confirms that many business programs require Social Security numbers, credit history, or citizenship, which excludes undocumented and newly arrived immigrants from financial support.

---

# **2\. LIMITED ACCESS TO FINANCIAL CAPITAL**

### **A. Immigrants rely heavily on personal savings instead of bank loans**

**Quote:**  
 “Immigrant-owned businesses rely more heavily on personal and family savings and are less likely to receive bank loans.”  
 (Fairlie, SBA 2012\)  
 🔗 [https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/Immigrant-Entrepreneurs-Financial-Capital-Full-Report.pdf](https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/Immigrant-Entrepreneurs-Financial-Capital-Full-Report.pdf)

**Analysis:**  
 Banks approve fewer loans for Latino and immigrant founders, forcing them to depend on relatives or informal lenders. This greatly limits how large and how fast their businesses can grow.

---

### **B. Latino entrepreneurs experience systemic discrimination in lending**

**Quote:**  
 “Minority-owned firms face higher loan denial rates and receive smaller loans even with identical creditworthiness.”  
 (Fairlie and Robb 2008\)  
 🔗 [https://www.mbda.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/files-attachments/DisparitiesinCapitalAccessReport.pdf](https://www.mbda.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/files-attachments/DisparitiesinCapitalAccessReport.pdf)

**Analysis:**  
 Even when immigrants have the same credit scores or qualifications as white applicants, they still receive fewer and smaller loans. This shows that financial exclusion is not about merit but about structural discrimination.

---

### **C. Nearly half of Mexican immigrants lack credit history**

**Quote:**  
 “Nearly half of Mexican immigrants report having no credit history upon arrival in the United States.”  
 (Migration Policy Institute 2024\)  
 🔗 [https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/mexican-immigrants-united-states](https://www.migrationpolicy.org/article/mexican-immigrants-united-states)

**Analysis:**  
 Without credit, immigrants cannot qualify for loans, leases, or equipment financing. Credit invisibility is one of the biggest financial barriers preventing aspiring immigrant business owners from accessing capital.

---

# **3\. LANGUAGE AND CULTURAL BARRIERS**

### **A. English-only programs exclude immigrants from aid**

**Quote:**  
 “Many immigrants could not access COVID-19 relief programs because materials were only available in English.”  
 (American Immigration Council 2020\)  
 🔗 [https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/report/covid19-immigrant-entrepreneurs-languages](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/report/covid19-immigrant-entrepreneurs-languages)

**Analysis:**  
 If relief programs are not translated, immigrants cannot apply for aid, loans, or grants. This language exclusion applies not only to COVID relief, but to countless government and small business programs.

---

### **B. Latino entrepreneurs lack culturally relevant business education**

**Quote:**  
 “First-generation Latino entrepreneurs often lack access to culturally aligned business support and education.”  
 (Immigrants Rising 2025\)  
 🔗 [https://immigrantsrising.org/wp-content/uploads/Immigrants-Rising\_Navigating-Entrepreneurship-Research-Report\_2025.pdf](https://immigrantsrising.org/wp-content/uploads/Immigrants-Rising_Navigating-Entrepreneurship-Research-Report_2025.pdf)

**Analysis:**  
 Traditional U.S. business training often assumes English fluency and prior familiarity with U.S. business norms, leaving immigrants without adequate mentoring or culturally responsive support.

---

# **4\. SOCIAL AND RACIAL DISCRIMINATION**

### **A. Mexican and Central American immigrants are racialized as “illegal”**

**Quote:**  
 “The figure of the ‘illegal alien’ is an ideological construct that renders Mexican migrants a deportable and subordinate workforce.”  
 (De Genova 2004, p. 161\)  
 🔗 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3185238](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3185238)

**Analysis:**  
 De Genova shows how racialized stereotypes follow immigrants into economic spaces, affecting how customers, landlords, and banks perceive them. This racialization creates long-term economic inequality.

---

### **B. Latino-owned businesses receive fewer and smaller loans**

**Quote:**  
 “Latino business owners continue to face significant gaps in loan approval and loan size.”  
 (SBA 2024\)  
 🔗 [https://advocacy.sba.gov/2024/01/03/hispanic-business-owners-facts/](https://advocacy.sba.gov/2024/01/03/hispanic-business-owners-facts/)

**Analysis:**  
 This data proves that Latino businesses are systematically underfunded. Even creditworthy Latino entrepreneurs encounter unequal treatment in the financial system.

---

### **C. Immigrant businesses face discrimination from customers, landlords, and suppliers**

**Quote:**  
 “Latino immigrant businesses frequently encounter discrimination from customers, landlords, and service providers, limiting growth opportunities.”  
 (Rutgers SMLR)  
 🔗 [https://smlr.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/Documents/Centers/WJL/MN\_SBChallenges.pdf](https://smlr.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/Documents/Centers/WJL/MN_SBChallenges.pdf)

**Analysis:**  
 Daily discrimination blocks access to commercial leases, fair pricing, and customer trust. These are foundational requirements for successful entrepreneurship, making discrimination a major structural barrier.

# A Decade of Data Shows Latino Entrepreneurs Growing and Adapting

[https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/decade-data-shows-latino-entrepreneurs-growing-adapting](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/decade-data-shows-latino-entrepreneurs-growing-adapting)  
![][image5]

# Latino Entrepreneurs Are Thriving, but Access to Contracts and Capital Remains Challenging

# Latino Entrepreneurs Are Thriving, but Access to Contracts and Capital Remains Challenging

https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/latino-entrepreneurs-are-thriving-access-contracts-capital-remains-challenging  
![][image6]

Latino entrepreneurs play a major role in the U.S. economy: More than 3 million people are employed by nearly 350,000 Latino-owned businesses. These businesses are also the fastest-growing segment of the U.S. business population: From 2007 to 2019, the number of Latino-owned businesses grew by 34% while the number of White-owned businesses fell by 7%.

And many are bouncing back from the economic shock of the COVID-19 pandemic: Between 2019 and 2022, Latino-owned businesses reported median growth of 25%, compared with 9% for White-owned businesses.

These are some of the findings in the eighth annual [*State of Latino Entrepreneurship*](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/state-latino-entrepreneurship-2022) report from the [Stanford Latino Entrepreneurship Initiative](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/labs-initiatives/slei) (SLEI) at Stanford Graduate School of Business.

“Latino entrepreneurs continue to thrive, even during unprecedented times,” says Barbara Gomez-Aguinaga, the associate director of SLEI and one of the report’s authors. Yet, she adds, “they keep facing systemic disparities that impact the growth of their businesses, including unequal access to government and corporate contracts.”

The report is based on a national survey of more than 10,000 business owners, about half Latino and half non-Hispanic White. The respondents’ companies generated at least $10,000 in annual revenue and had at least one employee beyond the owner.

“The goal of our research is to understand the challenges and opportunities that Latino-owned businesses face,” Gomez-Aguinaga says. “We hope our research informs and inspires the actions of decision makers, including governments, corporations, and business owners themselves.”

Some of the key findings in this year’s report:

## Businesses are recovering from the pandemic.

As the pandemic enters its fourth year, Latino entrepreneurs are adjusting to the new economic landscape. “Even though the pandemic hit Latino-owned businesses harder, they were more likely than White-owned businesses to say they have recovered and are doing better than before the pandemic,” Gomez-Aguinaga says.

One indicator: The percentage of Latino-owned businesses reporting business-to-business sales almost doubled from 20% in 2020 to 38% in 2022\. Overall, almost one-quarter said they are doing better than before the pandemic, compared with less than one-fifth of White-owned businesses.

## The Great Resignation has challenged businesses of all sizes.

“The Great Resignation was not as severe as the media portrays it,” Gomez-Aguinaga says. But the report found that Latino-owned businesses of all sizes have had difficulty hiring and retaining workers.

Latino business owners were more likely to report that employee retention is challenging, and they took action to improve it. The survey found that Latino-owned businesses were more likely than White-owned businesses to increase compensation and benefits, make work hours and locations more flexible, improve company culture, and offer more training and development opportunities. More White-owned businesses than Latino-owned businesses reported not taking action to improve employee retention.

## Contracts present challenges and opportunities.

Although only 13% of Latino-owned businesses had government or corporate contracts in 2022, these deals can be an important source of stability and growth. The report found that Latino-owned businesses are slightly more likely than White-owned businesses to get contracts, yet those contracts tend to be significantly smaller. For example, federal contracts for White-owned businesses were more than 30 times larger, on average, than those for Latino-owned businesses.

In addition, securing the contracts takes longer: The procurement process for government contracts takes more than a year for 37% of Latino-owned businesses, compared with 27% of White-owned businesses.

# Legal

# **📘 LEGAL INFORMATION IMMIGRANT ENTREPRENEURS SHOULD KNOW**

A website section designed for Mexican, Central American, and other immigrant entrepreneurs navigating U.S. business \+ immigration systems.

---

# **1\. Business Formation Laws for Immigrant Entrepreneurs**

## **LLCs, Sole Proprietorships, and Corporations**

**You *do not* need U.S. citizenship or a green card to register a business.**  
 Entrepreneurs with ITINs (not SSNs) *can* form LLCs, corporations, and sole proprietorships in most states.

**Key Source:**

* IRS – Applying for an ITIN  
   [https://www.irs.gov/individuals/how-do-i-apply-for-an-itin](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/how-do-i-apply-for-an-itin)

**Why this matters:**  
 Immigrant entrepreneurs often mistakenly believe they are not allowed to own businesses. Legally, the U.S. lets *anyone* start a business as long as taxes are filed properly.  
 Your website can highlight this to empower undocumented, DACA, visa-holders, and mixed-status entrepreneurs.

---

# **2\. ITINs (Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers)**

Immigrant entrepreneurs *without Social Security numbers* can use ITINs to:

* Pay business taxes

* Open business bank accounts (some banks only)

* Apply for business licenses

* Legally form an LLC

**Key Source:**

* IRS – ITIN Overview  
   [https://www.irs.gov/individuals/individual-taxpayer-identification-number](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/individual-taxpayer-identification-number)

**Why this matters:**  
 Lack of SSN is a major barrier. Showing people that ITIN-based entrepreneurship is legal is essential.

---

# **3\. EINs (Employer Identification Numbers)**

Immigrant entrepreneurs — documented or undocumented — **can legally obtain an EIN from the IRS using an ITIN.**

**IRS EIN Application:**  
 [https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employer-id-numbers](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employer-id-numbers)

**Why this matters:**  
 EINs are needed to hire employees, open business bank accounts, and file business taxes.

---

# **4\. U.S. Immigration Pathways Related to Entrepreneurship**

These do **NOT** apply to workers — only *founders, innovators, or entrepreneurs with business potential.*

## **International Entrepreneur Rule (IER) — “Startup Parole”**

Allows immigrant founders to receive temporary permission to stay in the U.S. if their startup shows:

* High growth potential

* At least $250k investment from U.S. investors **OR**

* Significant public benefit

**Official U.S. Citizenship & Immigration Services page:**  
 [https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/humanitarian-parole/international-entrepreneur-parole](https://www.uscis.gov/humanitarian/humanitarian-parole/international-entrepreneur-parole)

**Why this matters:**  
 Many immigrants don’t know there *is* a founder-focused program. Though limited, it represents a pathway for some.

---

## **E-2 Treaty Investor Visa (for Certain Latin America Countries)**

Allows entrepreneurs to run a U.S. business if they invest a substantial amount.  
 **BUT:** Mexico *is* eligible, most Central American nations are not.

**USCIS E-2 Visa Page:**  
 [https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/e-2-treaty-investors](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/e-2-treaty-investors)

---

## **L-1 Visa for Business Owners Expanding to the U.S.**

Allows immigrant entrepreneurs who own a foreign business to open a U.S. branch.

**USCIS L-1 Overview:**  
 [https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/l-1a-intracompany-transferee-executive-or-manager](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/l-1a-intracompany-transferee-executive-or-manager)

---

## **O-1 Visa for Extraordinary Entrepreneurs**

For immigrant founders who demonstrate “extraordinary ability.”  
 Tech founders \+ social entrepreneurs often qualify.

**USCIS O-1 Visa:**  
 [https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/o-1-nonimmigrant-visa](https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/temporary-workers/o-1-nonimmigrant-visa)

---

# **5\. Business Banking \+ Credit Laws Affecting Immigrant Entrepreneurs**

## **Banks that Accept ITIN (No SSN Required)**

Under federal law, banks *may* accept foreign passports, ITINs, or consular IDs.

**FDIC Acceptable ID Guidelines:**  
 [https://www.fdic.gov/resources/consumers/consumer-news/2022-02.html](https://www.fdic.gov/resources/consumers/consumer-news/2022-02.html)

**Why this matters:**  
 Mexican/Central American immigrants are highly unbanked.  
 Your website can show which banks are “ITIN-friendly.”

---

## **Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) – Immigrant Borrowing Protections**

Immigrants applying for credit (business loans or credit cards) have federal protections against:

* Discrimination

* Unfair lending practices

**CFPB Immigrant Financial Rights:**  
 [https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/blog/immigrants-and-money/](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/about-us/blog/immigrants-and-money/)

---

# **6\. Licensing and Permit Requirements**

Certain professions require legal status or SSN (e.g., real estate agents, nurses, contractors in some states).

However, **many states now allow undocumented or ITIN-only applicants** to obtain licenses.

## **Example: California AB 2184 — “Business Licenses for All”**

Allows local governments to accept **ITINs** instead of SSNs for business licenses.

**Bill Text:**  
 [https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill\_id=201720180AB2184](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180AB2184)

**Why this matters:**  
 Mexican and Central American entrepreneurs in CA can legally obtain local business licenses regardless of status.

---

# **7\. Immigration Laws That Create Barriers for Entrepreneurs**

## **1996 IIRIRA (Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act)**

Created:

* The 3-year & 10-year re-entry bars

* Heavy penalties for unlawful presence

* Fear of interacting with government systems

**Summary:**  
 [https://www.congress.gov/bill/104th-congress/house-bill/2202](https://www.congress.gov/bill/104th-congress/house-bill/2202)

**Impact:**  
 Entrepreneurs avoid applying for loans, licenses, and credit due to fear of detection — a major structural barrier.

---

## **Public Charge Rule (Historical Versions)**

Sometimes penalized immigrants for using certain public benefits.  
 Created confusion and fear even among people who *did not* use benefits.

**USCIS Public Charge Info:**  
 [https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-processes-and-procedures/public-charge](https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-processes-and-procedures/public-charge)

**Impact:**  
 Even business programs offering training or grants were avoided by immigrants out of fear.

---

# **8\. Laws and Policies That Support Immigrant Entrepreneurs**

## **State “Right to an ITIN” Policies**

States like CA, NY, and IL allow immigrants to use ITINs for:

* Business licenses

* State tax filings

* Some financing programs

## **Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs)**

CDFIs are legally designed to offer loans to underserved and immigrant borrowers.

**U.S. Treasury CDFI List:**  
 [https://www.cdfifund.gov/programs-training/certification/cdfi](https://www.cdfifund.gov/programs-training/certification/cdfi)
